title: Automated accessible text with contrast-color()
note: New native CSS function landing in Chrome 147, Firefox 146, Safari 26. Takes any color, returns black or white — whichever hits WCAG 2 AA (4.5:1). One line replaces all manual dark/light text logic in design systems.
takeaways: color: contrast-color(var(--brand-color)) — one line for always-accessible text
Works with prefers-color-scheme for auto dark mode text
Mid-tones are still a weak spot for the WCAG 2 algorithm
No JS or Sass hacks needed anymore
subject: Accessibility

title: contrast-color() beyond black & white
note: Follow-up to contrast-color() basics. Two methods to go beyond black/white: (1) tint with color-mix() in oklch, 10-25% for light colors, 30-40% for dark; (2) style queries + @property + if() for full custom palette branching. Chrome 137+/Safari 26+ only for method 2.
takeaways: color-mix(in oklch, var(--bg) 10%, contrast-color(var(--bg))) — branded tinted text

title: Basic Economics — An Introduction to Thomas Sowell
note: An English-first summary of a Hebrew introductory lesson based on Thomas Sowell’s Basic Economics. It presents economics as the study of choices under scarcity and emphasizes incentives, opportunity costs, and judging policy by results rather than intentions. This is a market-liberal interpretation of the book, not a neutral survey of economic consensus.
takeaways: Economics is not only about money, banks, or markets; it studies how limited resources with alternative uses are allocated.
Every choice has an opportunity cost: time, money, attention, and energy used for one thing cannot be used for another.
To evaluate policy, examine the incentives it creates and its actual results, not only the intentions behind it.
People respond to costs and rewards, so systems that ignore incentives can produce outcomes opposite to their stated goal.
Scarcity remains even in wealthy societies; relative abundance does not remove the need to choose and prioritize.
The lesson uses Milton Friedman’s example to argue that care and accountability may fall when people spend others’ money on others.
The video presents a pro-market ideological position. A future blog post should compare its claims with economists from other traditions.
Blog angle: why good intentions are not enough—and how incentives and unintended consequences shape policies and products.
subject: Economics
bias_note: The video presents a pro-market interpretation of Thomas Sowell’s work, not a neutral survey of economic consensus.
blog_angle: Why good intentions are not enough—and how incentives and unintended consequences shape policies and products.
takeaway: Economic rules shape everyday choices, so judging incentives and real outcomes helps people evaluate policies more carefully.

young_reader.summary: Economics studies decisions about limited resources such as money, time, materials, and work. People cannot have everything at once. Imagine you have 50 shekels and two free hours. You can buy a game, save the money, study, or meet a friend, but you cannot do all of them at the same time. Scarcity means that money, time, and other useful things are limited. An opportunity cost is what you give up when you make a choice. Incentives are rewards or costs that can change what people decide to do. These ideas can help us ask better questions about school rules, prices, and government plans. We should look at what a rule was meant to do and what happened after people reacted to it. A result that no one planned is called an unintended consequence. The video explains these ideas from a pro-market point of view. Other economists may agree with some parts and disagree with others, so readers should compare more than one source.
key_points: Scarcity means useful resources such as money and time are limited.
An opportunity cost is the best thing you give up when you choose something else.
Incentives are rewards or costs that can influence behavior.
Rules can create unintended consequences—results that nobody planned.
The source uses a pro-market viewpoint, so readers should compare it with other economic perspectives.
activities: Choice log: write down three choices you make today and what you give up with each choice.
Incentive map: choose one school rule. List its reward or cost, the behavior it encourages, and one result nobody may have planned.
Compare sources: find another introduction to opportunity cost. Write one point both sources agree on and one point they explain differently.
young_reader.quality_note: Adaptable for grades 7–9. The economic concepts are useful, but the original lesson is politically opinionated. This version adds concrete examples, defines key terms, labels the pro-market viewpoint, and asks readers to compare another source.

claims.claim: Scarcity means that people have more wants than the available goods, services, resources, and time can satisfy.
claims.label: Verified
claims.note: This is a standard introductory definition of scarcity in economics.

citations.title: What Is Economics, and Why Is It Important?
citations.evidence: Scarcity means that human wants for goods, services and resources exceed what is available.

claims.claim: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative that is given up when a choice is made.
claims.label: Verified
claims.note: This matches the standard textbook definition and is appropriate for the young-reader explanation.

citations.title: How Individuals Make Choices Based on Their Budget Constraint
citations.evidence: In short, opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative.

claims.claim: Changes in rewards, costs, prices, or other incentives can influence how people behave.
claims.label: Verified
claims.note: Microeconomics studies these responses, but the direction and size of an effect depend on the people and situation.

citations.title: Microeconomic and Macroeconomic Matters
citations.evidence: Microeconomics helps us understand incentives and behavior, consumer choices and consumption, and supply and demand.

claims.claim: Milton Friedman’s four-ways framework says people are least careful when spending someone else’s money on someone else.
claims.label: Viewpoint
claims.note: The citation verifies that Friedman presented this framework. It does not by itself prove that the framework predicts every public-spending decision.

citations.title: Milton Friedman — The Four Ways to Spend Money
citations.evidence: So there are four ways in which you can spend money.

claims.claim: Private organizations are always more efficient than public organizations.
claims.label: Disputed
claims.note: The evidence does not support an absolute rule. Outcomes vary across sectors and countries, and competition, regulation, market structure, and incentives can matter as much as ownership.

citations.title: Privatisation in Sub-Saharan Africa: Where Do We Stand?
citations.evidence: In the competitive manufacturing and tradable services sectors, efficiency gains, defined as improved performance of the company, have been generally achieved with wide variations in performance across firms and countries.

citations.title: Is Privatization Necessary?
citations.evidence: Neoclassical economic theory suggests that the relationship between ownership and performance is tenuous; efficiency is seen mainly as a function of market and incentive structures.

rubric.source_diversity: The original lesson represents a strong market-liberal viewpoint. The review adds an open textbook, OECD evidence, and a World Bank analysis, but a future article should also include a contemporary source representing another economic tradition.
rubric.missing_context: The source moves from useful basic concepts to broad claims about government, socialism, and private efficiency. Those conclusions need sector-specific evidence and competing explanations.
rubric.bias_framing: Scarcity, opportunity cost, and incentives are standard concepts. Friedman’s spending framework and blanket public/private efficiency claims must remain labeled as viewpoints or disputed claims.
rubric.reading_level: The standard summary measures grade 15.5. The parallel Young Reader version measures grade 7.2 and defines its key terms.
rubric.child_suitability: The foundational concepts are suitable for grades 7–9 after adaptation. The full source is not recommended as a neutral children’s lesson because it mixes instruction with political advocacy.
rubric.actionability: The item includes a choice log, an incentive map, and a compare-sources activity. The comparison activity should use one of the cited textbook or institutional sources.

decision.reason: The core economic concepts are accurate and useful, but a publishable article needs clearer separation between textbook concepts and ideological conclusions, plus stronger source balance.
required_revisions: Add inline citations to the definitions of scarcity, opportunity cost, and incentives.
Present Friedman’s four-ways framework as his argument, not as a proven universal law.
Replace any claim that private organizations are always more efficient with a sector-specific explanation of ownership, competition, regulation, and incentives.
Add one credible contemporary source from a different economic perspective before publication.
Keep the original video link and explain that it is the source being summarized, not the sole authority for the article.
